you visible warning signs of a heart
attack months or even years before one
ever actually happens? The shocking
thing is most people and even most
doctors never fully connect these
visible signs back to the heart. Today I
want to walk you through seven signs
that you can actually see and feel that
are associated with elevated
cardiovascular risk because knowing what
each of these signs are can save you
from a fatal event. Let me start with
the one I see most often in my clinic.
Take a look in the mirror. If you see
small yellowish slightly raised patches
around the eyelids or the inner corners
of the eyes, these may be xanthelasma.
Now, many people assume that these are
simply a cosmetic issue related to
getting older and while that sometimes
is true, xanthelasma is also a
well-documented marker of elevated
cholesterol and elevated cholesterol in
non-insulin sensitive individuals can be
a serious problem when it comes to heart
disease. Research published in the
European Heart Journal followed
thousands of patients over multiple
decades and found that people with
xanthelasma had a significantly higher
risk of heart attack and this held true
even in people whose cholesterol levels
on standard blood work appeared only
mildly elevated. The reason this matters
so much is that xanthelasma can
sometimes appear before a standard lipid
panel would flag anything concerning
which means the visible sign on your
face may be ahead of what shows up in
your blood work. If you see these
forming in yourself, this should prompt
you to ask your doctor for a full lipid
panel including apoB and particle based
testing if available, not just looking
at LDL and total cholesterol. Sign
number two is my personal favorite on
this entire list because it shocked my
third-year med school preceptor when I
knew what it was the moment she pointed
it out to me. Sign number two is called
arcus senilis and it looks like a thin,
pale, gray, or white ring forming around
the iris or the colored part of the eye.
It occurs due to lipid deposits around
the eye. And much like the first sign,
it may be a sign that a person's
cholesterol is too high, leading to
increased cardiovascular risk. In people
over 60, this is fairly common and not
always 100% concerning on its own. But
if you do have this, I highly encourage
you to get that full lipid panel we
talked about before. The third sign may
be a bit unusual, but it's been studied
extensively in the cardiovascular
research, and it's generally referred to
as Frank sign. Frank sign describes a
diagonal crease running across the
earlobe. And multiple studies have found
a correlation between this crease and an
increased risk of coronary artery
disease. The proposed mechanism is that
the same small blood vessel changes and
reduced blood flow that damage the
coronary arteries can also affect the
tiny vessels supplying the earlobe,
leading to a loss of the underlying
tissue elasticity that normally keeps
the earlobe nice and smooth. This is not
diagnostic on its own, but in
combination with other risk factors,
it's been consistently associated with
higher rates of cardiovascular events in
multiple independent studies. Now,
before we get into the signs that you
can see on your hands and your fingers,
several of which are commonly mistaken
as other medical conditions, if this
video is already starting to change the
way you're looking for warning signs of
heart disease, please consider
subscribing as it truly does help push
this information out to the people that
genuinely need to hear it the most. Sign
number four is a change of the
fingertips and the nails themselves,
where the nail begins to curve more over
the end of the fingertips, and the angle
between the nail and the skin becomes
less obvious. This is called clubbing of
the fingernails, and it's sometimes
described as the fingertip looking like
an upside down spoon. Nail clubbing is
classically associated with chronic low
oxygen levels in the blood, and while
it's more commonly linked to lung
conditions, it can also occur with
certain forms of congenital heart
diseases and infective endocarditis,
which is an infection of the heart
valves. This particular sign should
never be self-diagnosed from a video. If
you notice this change developing over
weeks or months, that warrants a prompt
medical evaluation, since the underlying
causes range from serious to very
serious. Sign number five are small
splinter-like marks underneath the
nails. These appear as thin
reddish-brown lines running vertically
under the nail, and they're known as
splinter hemorrhages. While a single
splinter hemorrhage on one finger is
often benign and can result from a minor
trauma to the nail, multiple splinter
hemorrhages appearing across several
fingers without any clear injury is a
recognized sign associated with
infective endocarditis, a serious
infection of the heart valves that
require medical attention. The
distinguishing feature is the pattern.
If it's only on one finger after you
slammed it in a car door, it's not
anything serious, but several appearing
spontaneously across multiple fingers is
a same-week doctor-wait, not just a
wait-and-see situation. Sign number six
is one of the more commonly recognized
signs, but most people attribute it to
either standing too long or having poor
circulation and not connecting it back
to the heart specifically. Peripheral
edema, swelling caused by fluid
retention in the lower legs and ankles,
can be an early sign that the heart is
not pumping efficiently enough to keep
fluid moving properly throughout the
body. This is a pattern we classically
see in congestive heart failure. The
distinguishing feature worth watching
for is whether the swelling is new,
whether it's present on both legs
symmetrically, and whether it comes with
any shortness of breath, particularly
while lying flat. This phenomenon is
called orthopnea, and that combination
specifically warrants a conversation
with your doctor about your heart's
pumping function. If you see swelling
that's asymmetric, or one leg is more
swollen than the other, it's probably
not due to congestive heart failure.
Sign number seven is a bluish tint
around your lips or your fingers, which
is known as cyanosis. This color appears
when blood oxygenation levels drop below
a certain threshold. While this can have
several causes, including lung
conditions, it can also indicate that
the heart is struggling to pump
adequately oxygenated blood throughout
the body, particularly in cases of
significant heart failure or in certain
congenital heart defects. This is one of
the more urgent signs on this list. If
you have new onset bluish discoloration
around the lips or fingertips,
especially if it comes on suddenly or
it's associated with either shortness of
breath or chest discomfort, this
warrants emergency evaluation. Now,
individually, each of these seven signs
alone may not totally represent
something wrong with your heart, but if
